Adult Santer seabream reach a maximum standard length of 75 cm [Li = 75 cm], a size that positions this sparid among the larger members of its family in the southwestern Indian Ocean. Field surveys indicate that the heaviest individuals attain an ultimate wet weight of 6900 grams [Wwi = 6900 grams], a figure derived from length–weight regressions based on extensive capture data across the Agulhas Bank. In contrast to these maximal dimensions, newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00022 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00022 grams]. This minute initial mass, comparable to that of other sparids with similar egg diameters, reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the yolk-sac larva during its lecithotrophic phase before first exogenous feeding is initiated.

The onset of sexual maturity in Cheimerius nufar is closely tied to body size, with puberty occurring once individuals reach a standard length at puberty of 34.6 cm [Lp = 34.6 cm]. At this developmental milestone, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 659 grams [Wwp = 659 grams], indicating that roughly ten percent of the ultimate body mass is required before gonadal recrudescence begins. This size-based threshold contrasts with some congeneric sparids that mature at proportionally larger sizes relative to their maximum length, suggesting that Santer seabream may adopt a somewhat earlier maturation strategy given the environmental conditions of its temperate reef habitat. Such patterns have implications for understanding the species' resilience to fishing pressure.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C], the maximum reproductive output of individual Santer seabream has been documented through a combination of fecundity and spawning frequency data. Gravid females release between 1,300 and 1,400 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 1,300 and 1,400 eggs per spawning event], with such spawning events occurring at a rate of roughly 1 spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly 1 spawning event per day] during the peak of the breeding season. This high daily reproductive rate, when integrated over the entire spawning period, yields an impressive total annual fecundity that underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover under favorable thermal regimes.

Longevity records for Cheimerius nufar indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 23 years [am = approximately 23 years], a value consistent with the life-history strategy of a moderately long-lived, iteroparous sparid inhabiting subt at a temperature of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C]ropical waters. These records, primarily derived from otolith annulus counts of the oldest individuals captured in commercial fisheries, were obtained from fish collected in waters maintained at a stable temperature of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C], reflecting the thermal regime of the Agulhas Current region. The species' extended lifespan, coupled with its early maturation and high fecundity, suggests a life-history that balances reproductive output against the risks of natural mortality in a variable reef environment.

Morphometric analyses reveal a steep allometric relationship between length and mass in Santer seabream, with the length–weight exponent exceeding a value of three, indicating a slightly positively allometric growth pattern where individuals become heavier per unit length as they approach their asymptotic size of 75 cm [Li = 75 cm]. This growth trajectory, typical of many demersal sparids, ensures that the wet weight at puberty of 659 grams [Wwp = 659 grams] is achieved well before half of the ultimate length is attained, allowing a substantial period of adult somatic growth that continues alongside reproductive activity. The 0.00022 gram [Wwb = 0.00022 gram] wet weight at birth represents an initial mass that is amplified by more than seven orders of magnitude over the course of the fish's lifespan, a remarkable ontogenetic scaling that underscores the species' capacity for efficient food conversion.
